=== Morphological Assessment Form ===
A. Leaf Arrangement & Architecture
    1. Leaf relative position (alternate / opposite / whorled): whorled (multiple leaves clearly attached at a single node, visible in close-up images)
    2. Leaf spacing (clustered / distal): clustered (leaves are tightly grouped at the shoot apex, forming a rosette-like arrangement)

B. Leaf Complexity
    3. Leaf complexity (simple / compound): simple (each leaf is a single blade without subdivisions)
    4. Compound leaf type, ONLY if leaf complexity is compound (odd-pinnate / even-pinnate): N/A (leaf complexity is simple)
    5. Number of leaflets (integer estimate 2, 4, 8, …): N/A (leaf complexity is simple)
    6. Leaflet arrangement (opposite / alternate / subopposite): N/A (leaf complexity is simple)

C. Leaf Morphology
    7. Leaf margin (entire / toothed) AND if toothed (dentate, serrate, etc.)): entire (margins are smooth without teeth or lobes)
    8. Leaf shape (elliptic, obovate, lanceolate, etc.): elliptic (broadest near the middle, tapering to both ends)
    9. Leaf apex (acute, obtuse, acuminate): acute (tip is sharply pointed)
    10. Leaf base (rounded, cordate, cuneate): rounded (base is gently curved, not tapering or lobed)
    11. Venation type (pinnate / palmate / parallel): pinnate (primary veins extend from midrib to margin, secondary veins branch off midrib)
    12. Secondary veins (visibility, spacing, number): visible, widely spaced, 4–6 per side (secondary veins are prominent, arching from midrib to margin, with 4–6 on each side)
    13. Leaf surface features (glabrous, shiny, dull, rugose): shiny (surface has a glossy appearance, reflecting light)
    14. Leaf surface trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs or fuzz on leaf surface)
    15. Petiole length (short / long): short (petioles are short, attaching leaves close to stem)
    16. Petiole features (winged / grooved / terete): terete (petioles are round in cross-section, not flattened or winged)

D. Stem & Shoot Traits
    17. Stem type, may not be visible (woody / herbaceous): woody (stem appears firm and slightly thickened, with visible lenticels and bark-like texture)
    18. Stem trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs on stem surface)
    19. Stem color: green with white patches (stem is primarily green, with irregular white or pale areas, possibly lichen or fungal growth)
    20. Stem texture (smooth / ridged / lenticellate): lenticellate (small, raised, corky spots are visible on stem surface)

    21. Stipules, sometimes visible only in close-up images (present / absent): absent (no stipules observed at leaf base)

rag_matches.description: Dioecious shrub or tree, to 15 m tall; trunk slender or to 20 cm dbh and deeply invaginated; stems sericeous when very young, glabrate in age, with conspicuous leaf scars. Leaves somewhat clustered at apex of branchlets; stipules caducous, to 1 cm long, sericeous, leaving a conspicuous interpetiolar line of trichomes; petioles 6-14 mm long, sericeous to glabrate; blades ovate-elliptic to obovate-elliptic, abruptly short-acuminate, usually obtuse and ± decurrent onto petiole at base, 7-13(21) cm long, 3.5-8 (12) cm wide, glabrous or with sparse long trichomes on major veins below and tufts of trichomes in axils, the margins ciliate and ± revolute.

Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Life Form: Tree, Shrub, Small Tree 
90. Posoqueria Aubl. By C.M. Taylor. Trees, small trees or terrestrial shrubs, unarmed, the flowers bisexual. Opposite leaves, isophyllous, entire, without domatia, the tertiary and higher order veins little visible on the underside or not visible; interpetiolar stipules, lanceolate to elliptical or oblanceolate, caducous, blunt to acute, flattened in bud. Terminal inflorescences, corymbiform, few-flowered to many-flowered, bracteate, upright to deflexed, the cimosal axes. Pedicellate flowers, bisexual, homostylous and apparently protandrous; calyx limb briefly 5-lobed, without calycophylls; corolla hypocratemeric with a slender and elongated tube (generally 2-4 mm in diameter), in bud more or less straight or with all lobes deflexed, white sometimes turning yellow after anthesis, glabrescent to papillose inside and often hirtellous in the throat and on the bases of the lobes, the lobes 5, quincuncial in bud, sometimes unequal in size in one flower, without appendage; anthers 5, exserted on developed and sometimes unequal filaments, dorsifixed near the base, with a triangular and acute apical appendage and a basal appendage of varied shape; stigmas 2, linear, erect and slightly coherent, included, located near or above 1/2 of the corolla tube; ovaries (1)2-locular, the ovules numerous, axillary. Fruits in berries, fleshy to coriaceous, subglobose to ellipsoidal, brown, yellow or orange; seeds subglobose to angular, smooth, with aril cream to orange. 14 spp. Mexico to northern Bolivia, northeastern Argentina, Cuba, Jamaica. In fertile state, Posoqueria is often confused with Alibertia and Randia; both differ by having the convolute aestivation of the corolla and unisexual flowers, and are distinguished from Tocoyena which has convolute aestivation and subsessile anthers. In the sterile condition of Posoqueria, its identification is often avoided. The treatment presented here uses several different characters to separate the species in addition to those used by Steyermark (1967) or Macias (1988), particularly the size and shape of the corolla, the arrangement of the androecium, the fruit characters. Often only one fruit develops in an inflorescence. The floral biology of several species of Posoqueria is unusual, and is described in more detail in Taylor et al. (2011): the anthers are cohesive at anthesis in a central group with unequal and bent filaments under tension until the whole is altered by a pollinator, then the filaments pull the anthers explosively and the pollen is forcefully released. The unequal, flexed filaments of these species generally produce a bent flower in bud, with the corolla lobes deflexed about 10-40° in relation to the tube to accommodate the long filaments. This treatment is based on Taylor et al. (2011) and agrees with Dwyer (1980) and Macias (1988) but not with Steyermark (1967) in treating the name Posoqueria panamensis as a synonym of P. latifolia, with the plants previously included in P. panamensis (i.e., Burger and Taylor (1993) now separated into several species.

Dioecious, hemiepiphytic tree, to 10 m tall; trunk to 15 cm dbh; branches spiraled, stiff and spreading, densely rooting at the nodes, the roots often extending back to the host tree and enveloping the host tree for support; stems glabrous with prominent leaf scars; sap pale yellow to bright orange (in time), not copious. Petioles to 2 cm long; blades obovate, rounded at apex (sometimes acute to acuminate on juvenile leaves), acute to obtuse at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-10 cm wide, very thick, dark green and glossy above, dull below, coriaceous; veins indistinct, drying with many fine veins. Panicles stout, bracteated, divaricately branched, terminal; buds depressed-globose; pedicels stout, to 1 cm long; flowers thick, 5-parted, spreading at anthesis, to 4.5 cm diam, white to pink, the lobes often marked with maroon or magenta at base or apex; sepals 2, concave, unequal, persisting in fruit; petals 4-10, broadly oblong, 2-2.5 cm long; androecium of staminate flowers cushion-shaped, ca 1 cm wide and 5 mm high with numerous anthers; pollen white, granular, compressed in round or oval pouches ca 1 mm diam, embedded just beneath the sticky surface of the disk; pistillate flowers similar to staminate but the gynoecium divided into (4)9(15) segments, the petals falling soon after anthesis, the sepals closing. Capsules subglobose, 2.5-3 cm long, dehiscing into 5-9 parts at maturity; valves thick, ± spreading to expose the colorful mass of seeds; seeds numerous, reddish, curved-oblong, ca 5 mm long, embedded in a deeply divided, bright-orange aril. Frequent epiphyte in the forest or on exposed shorelines; epiphytic on rocks or on trees near the edge of the water. Plants are usually supported on tree trunks or large branches but the branches may grow into the top of the canopy. Apparently flowers and fruits sporadically throughout the year. Where plants occur along the shore, the branches usually root at the nodes with the roots hanging in the water. The pollen sacs of the staminate flowers burst under the slightest pressure, and abundant pollen oozes out (sometimes explosively). Several species of small bees, including Trigona spp., have been seen visiting the flowers. The geographical range of Symphonia globulifera extends from Nicaragua to Panama, probably to Colombia. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Colon, San Bias, Veraguas, Herrera, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Code (El Valle) and Panama (Cerro Campana), and from tropical wet forest in Code (La Mesa) and Panama.

Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Life Form: Tree, Shrub, Small tree, Vine 
94. Randia L. By D.H. Lorence. Shrubs, trees, or vines, frequently armed with paired spines, terrestrial (rarely epiphytic in R. matudae), dioecious or rarely with bisexual flowers (R. pterocarpa, R. mayana, R. oaxacana), generally with monopodial branching but rarely sympodial (R. laevigata). Leaves opposite, sometimes clustered in spurs, isophyllous, sometimes anisophyllous, entire, generally without domatia (present in R. laevigata); minor venation not lineolate; stipules interpetiolar and sometimes also intrapetiolar, sometimes with different shapes in the twigs and spurs, triangular, erect, persistent or deciduous, valvate or imbricate. Flowers axillary or ramal or rarely terminal, solitary or 2-12 and fasciculate, fragrant, with stipule-like bracts, possibly with secondary pollen presentation; calyx limb 5-lobed, without calycophylls; corolla hypocraeteriform, white turning yellow after anthesis, the lobes 5, convolute, without appendages; stamens 5, included, the anthers dorsifixed, sessile; stigma 1, clavate and shortly 2-lobed, or 2 elliptical, included and situated just above the anthers; ovary 1-locular, the ovules numerous, parietal. Staminate inflorescences axillary, terminal, cauliflorous or ramal, cymose, fasciculate or in solitary few-flowered, generally ebracteate. Staminate flowers sessile or pedicellate, fragrant, apparently with secondary pollen presentation at least sometimes; calyx limb truncate or 5-6-lobed, without calycophylls; corolla hypocraeteriform to funnel-shaped, white turning yellow after anthesis, the lobes (4, R. truncata) 5-6, convolute, without appendages; stamens (4, R. truncata) 5-6, the anthers basifixed or dorsifixed, partially exserted, sessile or subsessile; pistillode present, with style, with stigma 1, clavate and short to deeply 2-lobed, exserted or included. Pistillate flowers terminal, axillary, cauliflorous or ramal, solitary, ebracteate, sessile or rarely few (R. altiscandens, R. laevigata); calyx limb similar to the staminate; corolla similar to the staminate or frequently larger than it; staminodes present, included to partially exserted, in the form of reduced and abortive anthers; stigmas clavate, short to deeply 2-lobed with the lobes linear or sometimes clavate, partially exserted; ovary 1-locular, the ovules numerous, parietal. Fruits in berries, subglobose to ellipsoidal, generally yellowish, white, orange to brown, the pericarp leathery to woody, smooth or sometimes tuberculate or longitudinally ridged to winged, the pulp fleshy and frequently dark brown or black; seeds ellipsoidal to subcircular, compressed, smooth. 70 spp. United States [Florida and Texas] and Mexico to Argentina. Randia has been treated previously in a much broader and poorly defined sense. Here it is restricted to the neotropical species with pollen in tetrads; the paleotropical species previously treated in Randia are now treated in several genera not necessarily closely related, particularly Catunaregam Wolf, Atractocarpus Schltr. et K. Krause, and Aidia Lour. Randia is similar to Rosenbergiodendron with which it has been previously confused; see the comment under this genus.

Trees, rarely shrubs; cylindrical trunks, sometimes ribbed or ribbed-interlaced, often with gum, with bark normally scaly and rarely smooth; milky sap, sometimes almost absent in the trunk, rarely yellowish; branching sometimes sympodial (Pouteria); twigs with indumentum of mostly simple trichomes, but sometimes there are Malpighiaceous or dendritic trichomes; stipules normally absent, present in Pouteria (rarely), Ecclinusa, Chromolucuma. Simple leaves, alternate, generally spiral or distichous (Chrysophyllum, Micropholis), secondary venation pinnate or penninerved (Diploon, Micropholis) and tertiary sometimes scalariform (Pradosia, Ecclinusa, Chromolucuma), margin entire; petioles cylindrical thickened towards the base or bottle-shaped, rarely ribbed. Inflorescences are axillary, ramiflorous or cauliflorous, fasciculate, sometimes solitary flowers. Flowers actinomorphic, bisexual or unisexual; sepals in 3 types: 5 unequal, imbricate; 5-12 imbricate; or, 6 in 2 series of 3, valvate; corolla gamopetalous, rotate or tubular, 4-6 (9) lobes; stamens epipetalous 4-6 (12), staminodes sometimes present; gynoecium syncarpous, superior ovary, the locules 1-6 (15); axile placentation, ovules 1 (rarely 2) per locule, simple style. Fruits are berries, rarely drupaceous (Pradosia); seeds 1 to several, the testa hard, smooth, shiny and brown.
The family consists of 53 genera and 1100 species, pantropical; 11 genera and around 408 species in the Neotropics; 10 genera and around 62 species in CR; 3 genera and 12 species in LS. The family is most diverse in lowlands with very humid climates, mainly below 1000 m.
It is recognized by its tree habit, with simple, alternate leaves, without stipules (very rarely present in CR), leaves clustered towards the apex of the twigs, cylindrical petioles thickened towards the base and the presence of milky sap. Venation patterns are of great taxonomic importance, so a careful analysis of them provides much utility in identification, especially the tertiary venation often reticulate at various levels or scalariform. The small flowers show a very homogeneous appearance and are always axillary, generally in fascicles. The seeds are very distinctive for their shape, hardness, luster, and annular scar, the latter variable in shape among genera. The vegetative characteristics mentioned earlier could confuse this family, especially with those that have milky sap, with families such as Olacaceae, Apocynaceae (with alternate leaves), etc.; the inner bark and sap with an almond scent also help to recognize Sapotaceae.
Several species produce edible fruits of economic importance, such as sapote (Pouteria zapota), medlar or sapodilla (Manilkara chicle, M. sapota), caimito (Chrysophyllum cainito), etc. The latex of Manilkara zapota was the primary resource for chewing gum. It is well known that the wood of several species is preferred for its hardness and durability.

Simple leaves, alternate, generally spiral or distichous (Chrysophyllum, Micropholis), secondary venation pinnate or penninerved (Diploon, Micropholis) and tertiary sometimes scalariform (Pradosia, Ecclinusa, Chromolucuma), margin entire; petioles cylindrical thickened towards the base or bottle-shaped, rarely ribbed. Inflorescences are axillary, ramiflorous or cauliflorous, fasciculate, sometimes solitary flowers. The family consists of 53 genera and 1100 species, pantropical; 11 genera and around 408 species in the Neotropics; 10 genera and around 62 species in CR; 3 genera and 12 species in LS. The family is most diverse in lowlands with very humid climates, mainly below 1000 m.
It is recognized by its tree habit, with simple, alternate leaves, without stipules (very rarely present in CR), leaves clustered towards the apex of the twigs, cylindrical petioles thickened towards the base and the presence of milky sap.
